courses.title: Rehabilitation Engineering and Prosthetics
courses.description: Biomechanics of human movement, design of prostheses and orthoses, wheelchairs and mobility devices, assistive technology for sensory and communication impairments, and medical device regulation.

topics.title: Biomechanics of Human Movement
topics.summary: Kinematics and kinetics, gait analysis, joint forces and tissue mechanics.

material.heading: Gait and motion
material.body: Biomechanics applies mechanics to living systems. Kinematics describes motion (displacement, velocity, acceleration, joint angles) without considering forces; kinetics studies forces (ground reaction forces, joint moments, power). The gait cycle (heel strike to the next heel strike of the same foot) has a stance phase (~60% — initial contact, loading response, midstance, terminal stance, preswing) and swing phase (~40% — initial, mid and terminal swing), with double support periods; running removes double support and adds a flight phase. Gait analysis uses 3D motion capture (reflective markers and infrared cameras), force plates, electromyography and pressure mats; low-cost alternatives include video analysis and inertial measurement units (IMUs — accelerometers and gyroscopes) — practical in Nigeria. Temporal–spatial parameters: walking speed (a 'vital sign' of function), cadence, step and stride length. Energy cost of walking increases with amputation level (transfemoral > transtibial), guiding prosthetic design.
keyPoints: Higher energy cost with higher amputation

material.heading: Joint forces and tissue mechanics
material.body: Static equilibrium (ΣF = 0, ΣM = 0) and free-body diagrams calculate muscle and joint reaction forces; because muscles act with short moment arms, joint forces greatly exceed body weight (hip joint force about 2.5–3 times body weight in walking; more on stairs). A walking stick in the opposite hand reduces hip abductor force and joint load. Tissue mechanics: stress–strain behaviour of bone (anisotropic, stronger in compression than tension; Wolff's law — bone remodels according to loads; stress shielding by stiff implants causes bone loss), ligaments and tendons (viscoelastic — creep, stress relaxation, hysteresis; toe region of the stress–strain curve), cartilage (biphasic — load bearing by fluid pressurisation), and skin (pressure and shear cause pressure ulcers — interface pressure must be kept low in sockets and seating). Material choice for devices balances strength, stiffness, weight, fatigue resistance, biocompatibility and cost.
keyPoints: Stick in opposite hand reduces hip load

topics.title: Lower Limb Prosthetics
topics.summary: Socket design, suspension, knees and feet, alignment and low-cost prosthetic technology.

material.heading: Components
material.body: A lower limb prosthesis includes the socket (interface with the residual limb — the most critical component for comfort), suspension, pylon (endoskeletal tube) or exoskeletal shell, knee unit (for transfemoral), and foot. Transtibial sockets: patellar tendon bearing (PTB — loads pressure-tolerant areas: patellar tendon, medial tibial flare, anterior compartment; relieves pressure-sensitive areas: tibial crest, fibular head, distal end) and total surface bearing (TSB — distributes load over the whole limb, often with silicone liners). Transfemoral sockets: quadrilateral (ischial seat) and ischial containment designs. Suspension: supracondylar cuff straps, silicone liners with pins (shuttle locks), suction and vacuum systems. Knees: single-axis (simple, cheap), polycentric (stability, shorter limb in swing), weight-activated stance-control ('safety knee'), pneumatic/hydraulic swing control, and microprocessor knees (expensive). Feet: SACH (solid ankle cushion heel — cheap, durable, widely used in Africa), single-axis, multiaxial and dynamic response (energy-storing carbon fibre) feet.
keyPoints: PTB: load patellar tendon, relieve fibular head

material.heading: Alignment and appropriate technology
material.body: Bench, static and dynamic alignment position the socket relative to the knee and foot to achieve stability and efficient gait; misalignment causes gait deviations (e.g. excessive knee flexion, lateral trunk lean, circumduction, vaulting) and skin problems. Prosthetic fitting follows healing and residual limb shaping; volume changes over the first months require socket adjustments or replacements. Appropriate technology for low-resource settings: ICRC polypropylene technology (thermoformed sockets and components — durable, affordable, locally manufactured), the Jaipur foot (natural-looking, allows squatting and barefoot walking — culturally appropriate in many African and Asian settings), 3D-scanned and 3D-printed sockets, and local production of components to reduce costs. Challenges in Nigeria: few prosthetists and orthotists (training at institutions such as the Federal College of Orthopaedic Technology, Igbobi), imported component costs, and follow-up for repairs. Upper limb prostheses: body-powered (cable and harness — durable, affordable, give proprioceptive feedback) and myoelectric (EMG-controlled — better cosmesis and grip, costly, need charging).

topics.title: Orthoses and Seating
topics.summary: Orthotic principles, common orthoses, wheelchair design, seating and pressure management.

material.heading: Orthoses
material.body: Orthoses are externally applied devices that modify the structural and functional characteristics of the neuromuscular and skeletal systems — to support, align, prevent or correct deformity, protect, or improve function. They are named by the joints they cross: FO (foot orthosis), AFO (ankle–foot — foot drop, spasticity; rigid, hinged or posterior leaf spring), KAFO (knee–ankle–foot — quadriceps weakness, e.g. post-polio), HKAFO, TLSO (thoracolumbosacral — scoliosis, spinal fractures), CTO/cervical collars, WHO (wrist–hand — carpal tunnel, radial nerve palsy dynamic splints), and hand splints for burns. Biomechanical principle: the three-point pressure system (one force opposed by two counter-forces) controls joint motion; larger contact areas reduce pressure. Materials: thermoplastics (polypropylene — durable; low-temperature thermoplastics for quick splinting), metals, carbon composites and leather. Clubfoot braces (foot abduction orthosis) maintain Ponseti correction. Proper fitting avoids pressure sores, especially over insensate skin.

material.heading: Wheelchairs and seating
material.body: Wheelchair components: frame (folding or rigid), seat and backrest, cushions, wheels (large rear wheels with hand rims for self-propulsion; castors), brakes and footrests. Measurements: seat width (hip width plus about 2–5 cm), seat depth (buttock to back of knee minus 2–5 cm), seat height and footrest height, backrest height depending on trunk control. Posture and seating: a stable pelvis (neutral, level) is the foundation of good posture; lateral supports, headrests and tilt-in-space support people with poor trunk control (e.g. severe cerebral palsy). Pressure management: users with spinal cord injury need pressure-relieving cushions (foam, air cells, gel) and regular pressure relief (push-ups or leaning every 15–30 minutes). WHO's eight-step wheelchair service (referral, assessment, prescription, funding, product preparation, fitting, user training, follow-up and maintenance). Rough terrain three-wheeled designs and locally manufactured wheelchairs suit rural Nigeria. Powered wheelchairs and scooters help those unable to self-propel.

topics.title: Assistive Technology for Sensory and Communication Impairments
topics.summary: Hearing aids and cochlear implants, visual aids, AAC devices, and environmental control.

material.heading: Hearing and vision
material.body: Hearing aids amplify sound: components — microphone, amplifier (digital signal processing — frequency shaping, compression, noise reduction, feedback cancellation), receiver and battery; types — behind-the-ear (robust, suitable for children and hot humid climates), in-the-ear and completely-in-canal. Fitting uses audiograms and prescriptive formulas. Cochlear implants bypass damaged hair cells by electrically stimulating the auditory nerve via an electrode array in the cochlea, with an external processor and transmitter coil — for severe to profound sensorineural loss (e.g. after meningitis); a small number of Nigerian centres perform implantation; cost and follow-up are barriers. Bone-anchored hearing aids suit conductive loss and chronic ear discharge. WHO promotes affordable, solar-rechargeable hearing aids. Visual assistive technologies: spectacles and low-vision aids (magnifiers, telescopes), screen readers and text-to-speech software, Braille displays, white canes, and smartphone apps (object recognition, navigation).

material.heading: Communication and environmental control
material.body: Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) supports people who cannot rely on speech (cerebral palsy, autism, motor neurone disease, stroke with aphasia, laryngectomy): low-tech (picture boards, communication books), and high-tech speech-generating devices and tablet apps accessed by touch, switches (scanning), head pointers or eye-gaze tracking. Brain–computer interfaces translate EEG signals into commands for severely paralysed people (research stage). Environmental control systems allow users to operate lights, doors, fans, televisions and phones through switches, voice commands or apps — smart home technology increasingly lowers costs. Design principles: user-centred design (involving users and carers throughout), universal design (products usable by as many people as possible without adaptation), affordability, local repairability and cultural acceptability. Many devices are abandoned when they do not match users' needs, environments or priorities — careful assessment, training and follow-up reduce abandonment.

topics.title: Medical Device Design, Safety and Regulation
topics.summary: Design process, risk management, electrical safety, standards and regulatory pathways in Nigeria.

material.heading: Design and risk
material.body: Medical device design follows design controls: user needs, design inputs (requirements), design outputs, verification (did we build it right — meets specifications), validation (did we build the right thing — meets user needs, often through clinical evaluation and usability testing), design transfer to manufacturing, and design history file. Risk management (ISO 14971): identify hazards, estimate and evaluate risks (severity × probability), implement controls (inherent safety by design first, then protective measures, then information for safety), and assess residual risk. Usability engineering (IEC 62366) prevents use errors. Quality management systems for manufacturers follow ISO 13485. Devices are classified by risk (e.g. Class I low — walking sticks, bandages; Class II moderate — infusion pumps, hearing aids; Class III high — implantable devices such as pacemakers and cochlear implants; or classes A–D in some systems), which determines regulatory requirements.

material.heading: Electrical safety and regulation
material.body: Electrical safety (IEC 60601 series): protect against macroshock (current through the body — about 10 mA causes 'let-go' threshold problems, 100 mA can cause ventricular fibrillation) and microshock (small currents, as low as 10–100 µA, applied directly to the heart via catheters or pacing wires can cause VF). Protection: insulation (Class I devices with protective earth; Class II double insulation), isolated patient-applied parts (types B, BF, CF — CF for direct cardiac contact, the most stringent leakage limits), leakage current testing, and routine electrical safety inspections. Unstable power supply in Nigeria makes surge protection, voltage stabilisers, UPS and robust design important. Regulation: NAFDAC regulates registration, importation, manufacturing and post-market surveillance of medical devices in Nigeria; the Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) sets standards; the NNRA regulates radiation-emitting devices. International frameworks include the IMDRF, the EU MDR (CE marking) and US FDA pathways (510(k), PMA). Post-market surveillance and vigilance report adverse incidents and recalls. Donated equipment needs compatibility, spare parts and training to avoid becoming unused 'equipment graveyards'.
